True Statement: A tissue is a group of cells (similar in structure) that work together to perform a specific function.
False 1: A tissue is a group of different cells that work together to perform different functions.
False 2: An organ is a group of cells (similar in structure) that work together to perform a specific function.

True Statement: The formation of different types of tissues leads to the division of labour, which increases the efficiency of the body and enables it to carry out complex life processes.
False 1: The formation of different types of tissues leads to the centralisation of function, which decreases the efficiency of the body.

True Statement: In animals, muscle tissue enables movement and nervous tissue carries messages to different parts of the body.
False 1: In animals, nervous tissue enables movement and muscle tissue carries messages to different parts of the body.
False 2: In animals, epithelial tissue enables movement and connective tissue carries messages to different parts of the body.

True Statement: In plants, xylem transports water and minerals, while phloem transports food.
False 1: In plants, phloem transports water and minerals, while xylem transports food.

True Statement: Plants have growth zones at the tips of their roots and shoots, called the apical meristems, which help the plants grow in length.
False 1: Plants have growth zones at the tips of their roots and shoots, called the lateral meristems, which help the plants grow in length.
False 2: Plants have growth zones at the base of their internodes, called the apical meristems, which help the plants grow in length.

True Statement: The increase in girth of the stem occurs due to the presence of actively dividing cells arranged in a ring in the stem; this meristematic tissue is called the lateral meristem.
False 1: The increase in girth of the stem is due to actively dividing cells arranged in a ring; this meristematic tissue is called the apical meristem.
False 2: The increase in length of the stem occurs due to actively dividing cells arranged in a ring; this meristematic tissue is called the lateral meristem.

True Statement: By counting annual growth rings, scientists can estimate the age of a tree and also understand the climatic conditions under which it grew.
False 1: By counting annual growth rings, scientists can estimate the depth of the roots of a tree.

True Statement: The intercalary meristem is located at the base of the internode or just above the node and helps grasses and similar plants regenerate after cutting or grazing.
False 1: The intercalary meristem is located at the tip of the shoot or root and helps grasses regenerate after cutting.
False 2: The lateral meristem is located at the base of the internode and helps grasses regenerate after cutting.

True Statement: Plants have three types of meristematic tissues — apical, lateral and intercalary.
False 1: Plants have two types of meristematic tissues — apical and lateral only.
False 2: Plants have three types of meristematic tissues — apical, lateral and permanent.

True Statement: The apical meristem increases length; the lateral meristem increases girth; the intercalary meristem at the base of certain plants helps them regenerate after cutting.
False 1: The apical meristem increases girth; the lateral meristem increases length; the intercalary meristem helps plants regenerate.

True Statement: The cells of meristematic tissues are small, have thin cell walls, a large and prominent nucleus, and dense cytoplasm; vacuoles are generally absent and cells are tightly packed with little or no intercellular space.
False 1: The cells of meristematic tissues are large, have thick cell walls, a small nucleus, and sparse cytoplasm; large vacuoles and many intercellular spaces are present.
False 2: The cells of meristematic tissues have large vacuoles that store nutrients, and are loosely packed with many intercellular spaces.

True Statement: The process by which meristematic tissue becomes specialised to perform specific functions is called differentiation; cells that lose the ability to divide become permanent tissues.
False 1: The process by which meristematic tissue becomes specialised to perform specific functions is called dedifferentiation.
False 2: All newly formed meristematic cells remain meristematic and none lose the ability to divide.

True Statement: Permanent tissues can be simple (composed of only one type of cell) or complex (composed of more than one type of cell).
False 1: Permanent tissues are always simple, composed of only one type of cell.
False 2: Meristematic tissues can be simple (one type of cell) or complex (more than one type of cell).

True Statement: The epidermis forms the outermost layer of the plant body; it consists of a tightly packed, single layer of flat and rectangular cells.
False 1: The epidermis forms the innermost layer of the plant body.
False 2: The epidermis consists of loosely packed, multiple layers of irregularly shaped cells.

True Statement: Epidermal cells are covered with a waxy layer of cutin called the cuticle; in plants living in very dry habitats, the epidermis may be covered by a thick layer of cuticle to reduce water loss.
False 1: Epidermal cells are covered with a waxy layer of lignin called the cuticle.
False 2: In plants living in very dry habitats, the cuticle is thin to allow maximum water absorption.

True Statement: In roots, hair-like projections from epidermal cells are called root hair, which increase the surface area for absorption of water and minerals from the soil.
False 1: In roots, hair-like projections from epidermal cells are called root hair, which decrease the surface area for absorption.
False 2: In stems, hair-like projections from epidermal cells are called root hair, which increase surface area for absorption.

True Statement: In leaves, the epidermis contains pores called stomata, which help in gaseous exchange and transpiration (evaporation of water vapours).
False 1: In roots, the epidermis contains pores called stomata, which help in gaseous exchange and transpiration.
False 2: In leaves, the epidermis contains pores called lenticels, which help in gaseous exchange and transpiration.

True Statement: Transpiration helps in water transportation by creating a transpiration pull in xylem; transpiration also helps in elimination of wastes from the plant body.
False 1: Transpiration helps in water transportation by creating a transpiration pull in phloem.

True Statement: In young plants, the outer protective layer is a single-layered epidermis; as plants grow older, some cells below the epidermis develop the ability to divide and form the cork cambium.
False 1: In old plants, the outer protective layer remains a single-layered epidermis that does not change.

True Statement: Cork cells are dead, compactly arranged, and contain a substance which makes them impermeable to water and gases; this forms the bark of the tree.
False 1: Cork cells are living, loosely arranged, and contain a substance that makes them permeable to water and gases.
False 2: The division of cork cambium cells gives rise to parenchyma cells that form the bark of the tree.

True Statement: There are three types of simple permanent tissues: parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma.
False 1: There are two types of simple permanent tissues: parenchyma and collenchyma only.

True Statement: Parenchyma consists of living cells with thin walls; these cells are loosely packed with intercellular spaces; parenchyma mainly stores food but also performs photosynthesis in the green parts of plants.
False 1: Sclerenchyma consists of living cells with thin walls and loosely packed intercellular spaces, and mainly stores food.
False 2: Parenchyma consists of dead cells with thick walls; these cells are tightly packed without intercellular spaces.

True Statement: In aquatic plants, specialised parenchyma forms air spaces, which help them float.
False 1: In aquatic plants, specialised sclerenchyma forms air spaces, which help them float.
False 2: In aquatic plants, specialised parenchyma forms air spaces, which help them sink.

True Statement: Collenchyma consists of living cells with unevenly thickened corners due to pectin deposition; this tissue provides support and flexibility, allowing parts like stems and tendrils to bend without breaking.
False 1: Sclerenchyma consists of living cells with unevenly thickened corners due to pectin deposition and provides support and flexibility.
False 2: Collenchyma consists of living cells with unevenly thickened corners due to lignin deposition.

True Statement: Sclerenchyma cells have thick walls due to deposition of lignin, making them hard and strong; most of these cells are dead; this tissue is found in stems, leaf veins, and hard coverings of seeds and nuts.
False 1: Collenchyma cells have thick walls due to deposition of lignin, making them hard and strong; most of these cells are dead.
False 2: Sclerenchyma cells have thick walls due to deposition of pectin, making them hard and strong.

True Statement: Xylem transports water and minerals from the roots to other parts of the plant and also provides strength to the plant.
False 1: Phloem transports water and minerals from the roots to other parts of the plant.
False 2: Xylem transports food from the leaves to other parts of the plant.

True Statement: Xylem consists of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres; xylem parenchyma is the only living component of xylem, while tracheids, vessels, and xylem fibres are primarily sclerenchymatous.
False 1: Xylem consists of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres; tracheids and vessels are the only living components while xylem parenchyma and fibres are sclerenchymatous.
False 2: Phloem parenchyma is the only living component of xylem.

True Statement: Unlike xylem, phloem is mostly made up of living cells; it consists of sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres.
False 1: Unlike phloem, xylem is mostly made up of living cells; it consists of sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres.

True Statement: Sieve tubes transport food from leaves to other parts of the plant; the cellular functions of the sieve tube cells are regulated by companion cells.
False 1: Tracheids transport food from leaves to other parts of the plant.
False 2: Sieve tubes transport water and minerals from roots to other parts of the plant.

True Statement: Companion cells are specialised parenchyma cells whose main function is to monitor loading and unloading of sugars in sieve tubes.
False 1: Companion cells are specialised sclerenchyma cells whose main function is to monitor loading and unloading of sugars in sieve tubes.
False 2: Companion cells monitor loading and unloading of water in xylem tracheids.

True Statement: Phloem parenchyma stores food materials, resin, tannins and latex; phloem fibres are primarily sclerenchymatous and provide strength.
False 1: Xylem parenchyma stores food materials, resin, tannins and latex.
False 2: Phloem fibres are primarily parenchymatous and provide flexibility.

True Statement: Plant tissues are organised into three tissue systems: dermal tissue system (outer covering), ground tissue system (between dermal and vascular), and vascular tissue system (xylem and phloem).
False 1: Plant tissues are organised into two tissue systems: dermal and vascular only.

True Statement: Animal tissues are mainly of four types: epithelial, connective, muscular and nervous tissues.
False 1: Animal tissues are mainly of three types: epithelial, connective and muscular tissues only.
False 2: Animal tissues are mainly of four types: epithelial, connective, xylem and nervous tissues.

True Statement: Epithelial tissue forms the outer covering of the body (skin) and also lines internal organs such as the mouth, lungs, blood vessels and intestine; it is composed of closely packed cells with very little space between them.
False 1: Connective tissue forms the outer covering of the body and also lines internal organs; it is composed of closely packed cells with very little space between them.
False 2: Epithelial tissue is composed of loosely packed cells with large spaces between them.

True Statement: The red colour of blood is due to haemoglobin, an iron-rich protein in the Red Blood Cells (RBCs); RBCs live for about 4 months and are replaced regularly.
False 1: The red colour of blood is due to haemoglobin, a calcium-rich protein in the Red Blood Cells.
False 2: RBCs live for about 12 months and are replaced regularly.

True Statement: Platelets help in blood clotting at the site of injury.
False 1: White Blood Cells (WBCs) help in blood clotting at the site of injury.
False 2: Platelets help in oxygen transport at the site of injury.

True Statement: White Blood Cells (WBCs) collect at infected areas, causing pus formation and inflammation (redness and swelling).
False 1: Red Blood Cells (RBCs) collect at infected areas, causing pus formation and inflammation.
False 2: Platelets collect at infected areas, causing pus formation and inflammation.

True Statement: Blood is fluid, while bone is hard; this difference is due to the matrix, which is watery, soft and jelly-like in blood but hard, solid, and rigid in bones.
False 1: Blood is hard, while bone is fluid; the matrix is hard and rigid in blood but watery and jelly-like in bones.

True Statement: Bones have a rigid matrix containing calcium and phosphorus compounds, giving them strength and rigidity.
False 1: Bones have a rigid matrix containing potassium and nitrogen compounds, giving them strength and rigidity.
False 2: Cartilage has a rigid matrix containing calcium and phosphorus compounds, giving it strength and rigidity.

True Statement: Cartilage has a soft, jelly-like matrix and provides flexibility and cushioning.
False 1: Bone has a soft, jelly-like matrix and provides flexibility and cushioning.
False 2: Cartilage has a hard, rigid matrix and provides strength and rigidity.

True Statement: Tendons connect muscles to bones, while ligaments connect bones to bones and prevent excessive movement.
False 1: Ligaments connect muscles to bones, while tendons connect bones to bones and prevent excessive movement.

True Statement: Skeletal muscles are responsible for voluntary movements; they are made up of bundles of long, cylindrical cells (muscle fibres) that are unbranched, multinucleate (many nuclei) and striated.
False 1: Smooth muscles are responsible for voluntary movements; they are unbranched, multinucleate and striated.
False 2: Skeletal muscle fibres are branched, uninucleate (one nucleus) and lack striations.

True Statement: Smooth muscles are found in organs like the stomach and intestines; their cells are spindle-shaped, have a single nucleus and lack striations; they help in slow, continuous movements like digestion.
False 1: Skeletal muscles are found in organs like the stomach and intestines.
False 2: Smooth muscle cells are cylindrical and branched with a single nucleus and have faint striations.

True Statement: Cardiac muscles are found only in the heart; their fibres are cylindrical and branched with a single nucleus and have faint striations; cardiac muscles work tirelessly and rhythmically, enabling the heart to beat throughout life without fatigue.
False 1: Skeletal muscles are found only in the heart; their fibres are cylindrical and branched with a single nucleus.
False 2: Cardiac muscle fibres are spindle-shaped, unbranched, with a single nucleus and lack striations.

True Statement: The cells of nervous tissue are called neurons (nerve cells), which are specialised to receive, process and transmit messages; each neuron has three main parts: the cell body (contains nucleus), dendrites (receive signals from other neurons), and an axon (carries messages from the cell to axon terminals).
False 1: The cells of nervous tissue are called nephrons.
False 2: Dendrites carry messages from the cell to axon terminals, while the axon receives signals from other neurons.

True Statement: The axon terminals transmit messages to other cells.
False 1: The dendrites transmit messages to other cells.

True Statement: The musculoskeletal system is made up of bones, muscles, joints, cartilage, tendons and ligaments; it functions under the control of the nervous system.
False 1: The musculoskeletal system functions under the control of the endocrine system.

True Statement: On average, the adult human skeleton makes up about 12–15 per cent of body weight.
False 1: On average, the adult human skeleton makes up about 30–40 per cent of body weight.
False 2: On average, the adult human skeleton makes up about 1–2 per cent of body weight.

True Statement: The ball and socket joint (e.g., shoulder) allows forward, backward, sideways and circular movements.
False 1: The hinge joint (e.g., shoulder) allows forward, backward, sideways and circular movements.
False 2: The ball and socket joint allows movement in only one direction, like a door hinge.

True Statement: The hinge joint (e.g., elbow, knee) allows bending and straightening in one direction only; a small bone called the kneecap protects the knee joint.
False 1: The ball and socket joint allows bending and straightening in one direction only.
False 2: The hinge joint allows free movement in all directions including circular rotation.

True Statement: The skull is connected to the backbone through a pivot joint, which allows the head to move side to side.
False 1: The skull is connected to the backbone through a hinge joint, which allows the head to move side to side.
False 2: The elbow is connected to the upper arm through a pivot joint, which allows the forearm to move side to side.

True Statement: The bones of the skull are connected by fixed joints, which means the bones of the skull cannot move; this keeps the brain safe.
False 1: The bones of the skull are connected by hinge joints, allowing them to flex and protect the brain.
False 2: The bones of the skull are connected by fixed joints that allow the skull bones to move freely.

True Statement: The backbone (vertebral column) is made up of a series of small bones called vertebrae; it supports the body and helps us stand upright.
False 1: The backbone is made up of a series of small bones called carpals.
False 2: The rib cage is made up of a series of small bones called vertebrae and helps us stand upright.

True Statement: Between each vertebra is a cartilage disc, which acts as a cushion and allows flexibility so we can bend and twist without injuring the spinal cord.
False 1: Between each vertebra is a bone disc, which acts as a cushion and allows flexibility.
False 2: Between each vertebra is a cartilage disc that makes the spine rigid and inflexible.

True Statement: Humans have 12 pairs of ribs; together they form the rib cage, which protects vital organs such as the heart and lungs.
False 1: Humans have 10 pairs of ribs; together they form the rib cage.
False 2: Humans have 12 pairs of ribs forming the rib cage, which protects vital organs such as the kidneys and liver.

True Statement: The ribs are attached to the spine at the back and to the breast bone (sternum) in the front; they are joined by flexible cartilage, which allows the rib cage to expand and contract during breathing.
False 1: The ribs are attached to the spine at the back and to the collarbone (clavicle) in the front.
False 2: The ribs are joined by rigid bone, which keeps the rib cage fixed and prevents breathing movements.

True Statement: In 1958, F. C. Steward demonstrated that even single cells from the vascular phloem of carrot retain the ability to regenerate whole plants (totipotency).
False 1: In 1958, F. C. Steward demonstrated that single cells from the xylem of carrot retain the ability to regenerate whole plants.
False 2: In 1902, F. C. Steward demonstrated that single cells from the vascular phloem of carrot retain the ability to regenerate whole plants.

True Statement: In Steward's experiment, phloem cells first dedifferentiated to form an undifferentiated mass of unspecialised cells, which then redifferentiated to form roots, shoot, and the complete plant.
False 1: In Steward's experiment, phloem cells first differentiated (specialised) to form specific tissues, which then redifferentiated to form a complete plant.
False 2: In Steward's experiment, xylem cells first dedifferentiated to form an undifferentiated mass, then redifferentiated into a complete plant.
